description: [MÉDIA] 7 — Login returns the raw session token in the JSON body in addition to the httpOnly cookie, giving XSS a token to exfiltrate. INVESTIGATION ALREADY DONE (see below) — safe to implement, do NOT re-investigate and do NOT pause unless you find a consumer contradicting these findings. Independent of the other features.
steps: In src/auth/auth.controller.ts#login, keep the httpOnly signed-cookie behavior exactly as-is (setSessionCookie).

Change the returned `session` object: always return `session: { expiresAt: expiresAt.toISOString() }`. Include `token: sessionToken` ONLY when the caller signals Bearer intent: the incoming request already carries an `Authorization` header, OR sends an explicit opt-in header `x-auth-response-token: 1`. Read these from the `@Req() req` (add `@Req() req: Request` is already present in the handler).

Add a short code comment referencing finding [MÉDIA] 7 explaining that browser logins rely on the httpOnly cookie and must not receive the raw token, while server-to-server Bearer integrations opt in.
Do NOT modify src/auth/auth.service.ts session creation. Do NOT change the cookie format or name.
acceptance_criteria: A browser-style login (no Authorization header, no x-auth-response-token header) returns `user` and `session: { expiresAt }` WITHOUT `session.token`, and still sets the httpOnly cookie.
A login request carrying `x-auth-response-token: 1` (or an Authorization header) still returns `session.token` for the Bearer flow.
No existing spec breaks (there is no auth.controller.spec.ts; session-token/auth-guard specs are unaffected).
verification: pnpm exec tsc --noEmit — no new errors outside the baseline fiscal spec files.
findings: IMPLEMENTED: In src/auth/auth.controller.ts#login the httpOnly signed-cookie behavior (setSessionCookie / signSessionToken) is unchanged. The login response now always returns session:{ expiresAt: expiresAt.toISOString() } and conditionally spreads token:sessionToken ONLY when the request signals Bearer intent — computed as `const wantsResponseToken = req.headers['authorization'] !== undefined || req.headers['x-auth-response-token'] === '1'`. A code comment referencing finding [MÉDIA] 7 explains the rationale. auth.service.ts session creation and the cookie name/format were NOT touched. VERIFICATION: `pnpm exec tsc --noEmit` shows only the 23 baseline errors in src/fiscal/controllers/fiscal-apuracao.controller.spec.ts (1) and src/fiscal/services/fiscal-entregas.service.spec.ts (22) — no new errors. `pnpm test src/auth` = 19/19 passed (session-token.spec.ts, auth.guard.spec.ts). `pnpm build` succeeds. No auth.controller.spec.ts exists. ORIGINAL INVESTIGATION (Correction C): Browser consumer web/lib/auth-client.ts signIn.email() calls POST /api/auth/login with credentials:'include' and reads ONLY data.user — never data.session/data.session.token; session is maintained by the httpOnly cookie (getSession/useSession hit /api/auth/session with the cookie). The only session.token grep hits in web/ are Next.js HMR build artifacts, not app code. Bearer flow: src/auth/session-token.service.ts#extractBearerToken intentionally accepts the RAW DB session token as Authorization: Bearer <token>, and AuthService.validateSession looks it up by session.token — the raw sessionToken in the login body is exactly what a Bearer integration needs. The browser cookie uses a DIFFERENT signed format (token.hmac), so removing the body token does not affect the cookie flow. No auth.controller.spec.ts exists; no in-repo spec reads the login body session.token. Conclusion: conditioning the body token to Bearer-intent callers is safe and breaks nothing known. If a real browser/integration consumer reading session.token from the default response is discovered, PAUSE via send_message(warning) before changing the response shape.
